For a first world person such as myself, its easy to see libraries as unnecessary. Why do we need libraries when I can do almost all of what it features at home or elsewhere?

Physical books are a commodity that are now out of date due to the internet revolution. Why bother making the journey to a library when I could pull up a relevant pdf or the book itself online via an ebook shop? I really have no incentive to go for books when I can access books on my laptop, tablet, phone, gaming console, and even some wristwatches.

Sure, there are people who do not have access to these devices, but if that's so, then why the library? They should have a greater focus on establishing themselves with modern commodities. I'm sure you could buy an outdated iPod Touch or iPhone model for under $100 or even just steal one easily.

People who do not have a smart-phone really have no reason not to. I see people on welfare all the time buying gaming consoles. People are really dropping the ball if they have to go to a library.

Television is in the same situation with the books, but 3D printers? Not a lot of the general public have a use for that technology. If libraries were to lose funding, I'm sure there would be other places that one could go to 3D print (probably a university department).

Not that I actually believe any of the things I just said; just devil's advocate.

My main attraction of the library is that I can go there to provide myself an environment where I won't be distracted by all my modern luxuries. Its a good place for students like me who have little self-discipline.

Full Disclosure: I work as a librarian.

I'm glad to hear that you don't actually believe the positions you promote here, but I'd like to tackle them anyways, because there are people who sadly think this way.

Libraries are about more than books and information, but that's a section I'll touch upon later. Even if information or entertainment is the goal, simply having a smartphone is simply not enough of a reason to abolish libraries. When the time comes that you want information, access is key.

You might have access to a book via an e-copy, but you might not. There are still only a small percentage of the total realm of books being made into ebooks, so not every need is served by a digital platform on that alone. There's also the issue of cost. It costs money to get the device, to keep it in service, to charge it with electricity, and likely in the end to purchase the books or files you want to consume.

Do many homeless people have old smartphones? Yes, many do. But they don't necessarily have the ability to use them frivolously or for great deals of reading. There are other more vital needs for them, for example, being able to contact government offices for assistance, or in having a way to be contacted after applying for a job. You, as a well-off citizen may think nothing of tossing a few bucks to buy a book, but a homeless person confronted with the choice of buying a book to educate themselves and get a better chance at finding a job, or being able to eat today, is confronted with a different situation, and free access to information is something that becomes far more vital. The free access to information that libraries provide stop people from becoming forgotten and slipping through the cracks, they offer an opportunity to work for something better, even if you have no way to pay for it. That's a measure of civilization that is simply ignored by the private market.

Libraries go being just being warehouses of books and ebooks. They offer access to public computers and wi-fi, access that is vital for doing things as basic as applying for jobs, applying for unemployment, submitting insurance forms or paying your taxes. In fact, just look at taxes. It used to be that libraries would be sent physical copies of all the tax forms and instruction booklets, as would most city halls. These days almost none of them are sent, and instead are offered online. There are plenty of disadvantaged, elderly, and other people who lack the computers and/or home Internet to tackle these issues.

Libraries offer a safe place and a community space. It's not uncommon for children of working parents to come to the library as a safe place to be until their parents are out of work, without the library they would be wandering the streets or at home alone and unsupervised. Group activities are a way to bring people together and forge a community, and shared learning is particularly excellent for this.

Libraries are -centers- of learning for parents with children, both for parents to find new resources to help them raise their children well, and especially for children to begin learning early literacy skills that will have a major impact upon their success in life. Talk to a Kindergarten teacher, and ask them the difference between kids who have had reading experience and those that hadn't. It's a massive headstart to work on early literacy before school, and libraries have programs to begin the learning for any age, and supply a wealth of resources to parents and new readers.

You even mention 3D printers, and here I disagree as well. The public doesn't yet know -how- to handle that technology, that doesn't mean they don't have a use for it. They just don't understand what use they have for it yet. If you want to see just what a difference that can make, do a google search for '3d printed child prosthetic". You'll find that parents and kids have figured out ways to print up prosthesis for children that fit them better and more comfortably than traditional prosethetic devices, cost pennies on the dollar to produce, and can easily be upscaled and re-printed as they grow. To replace the traditionally uncomfortable, heavy, and unworldly devices for children who need them can change their entire childhood. As the technology advances it will be far more useful still. Jay Leno replaced an unfindable part for an antique car by scanning and printing a copy of a broken piece. 3D printing will revolutionize manufacturing in the next couple of decades, I think it's far too early to write it off as a tech not very useful to the public.

Libraries, ultimately, respond to the needs of their community. I've known libraries that checked out all sorts of non-book items, from bike locks for your visit to the library, to energy monitors to calculate home energy, fishing rods, musical instruments, telescopes, cake pans and far more. A well run library is a boon to any community in more ways than most people would ever imagine.
